operations.old: Originating from the physical sensors of electronic keyboards and pianos, MIDI velocity is a machine-centric measurement of physical intensity. To say it operates as a "note-level" parameter means that every music note from a discrete key strike is assigned an independent, static integer representing its initial strike force. This strict per-note measurement dictates that velocity functions as a discrete loudness control parameter. It is highly granular and absolute within its own scale, yet the resulting loudness highly depends on the acoustic environment and the specific instrument being played. Because MIDI velocity is necessary for MIDI-to-audio playback in DAWs and synthesisers, a common default is set to 64 when it is missing.
operations.new: Here, MIDI velocity refers to the velocity value in a Note On message. It is a machine-readable control parameter. In sensor-equipped piano data, the recorded value acts as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion. Each note carries an integer value that can be edited independently, although its acoustic effect depends on the instrument and renderer. When expressive values are missing, a MIDI sequence may instead use a constant such as 64.
